lecture11.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction

sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions

teaching.text: A **mass-spring system** is a mass hooked up to a spring, and its behavior comes from what each part "wants." **The spring wants to be at its equilibrium position**, which is its resting length, so if it is stretched or squished it pulls or pushes to get back there. **A mass that is moving wants to keep on moving**, so once it gets going it does not stop by itself.
children: When the mass is pulled out and let go, the spring pulls it back toward equilibrium. The mass is moving when it gets there, so it **keeps on moving** past equilibrium and squishes the spring.
The squished spring now pushes the mass back the other way, the mass overshoots again, and the cycle repeats. That repeating back and forth is **vibration**.
On a real table, **friction** slowly brings the motion to a stop. The model leaves friction out, so in the model the system vibrates forever.

teaching.text: The same system can move in **two directions**, and it is important to understand both kinds of motion, because some systems are easier to think about one way than the other.
children: In **longitudinal** motion, the mass moves **left and right**, back and forth along the line of the spring.
In **transverse** motion, the mass sits between **two walls** with a spring on each side, and it moves **up and down**, across the line of the springs.

teaching.text: **Both kinds of motion work in exactly the same way, and for the same reason.** Pulling the transverse mass up **stretches the springs**, and since springs hate being stretched, they pull the mass back down. As the mass passes the middle, the springs are not stretched at all, but the mass is still moving, so it keeps going and stretches them on the other side.
children: Both versions vibrate at the **same rate**, because they have the same mass and the same total stiffness in the direction of motion.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: **Frequency** is the number of back-and-forth cycles a system completes each second, and two things set it, the **mass** and the **stiffness**. Each change has the same effect in longitudinal motion and in transverse motion.

**A heavier mass vibrates more slowly.** A heavy mass is hard to get moving and hard to turn around, so each trip takes longer. **Heavy branches sway back and forth slowly, while little branches sway quickly.**
children: Making the mass **four times heavier cuts the rate in half**.

teaching.text: **A stiffer spring makes the system vibrate faster.** The stiffer something is, the harder it pulls back toward where it started, so it turns the mass around sooner.
children: Making the spring **four times stiffer doubles the rate**.

teaching.text: **Raising the mass lowers the frequency, and raising the stiffness raises the frequency.** Each part has its effect only while it is doing its job.
children: **A mass affects frequency by moving, and a spring affects frequency by stretching and compressing.** A mass that never moves could be made a thousand pounds heavier without changing the frequency at all, and a spring that never stretches adds no stiffness.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: With **two masses**, the system has two walls, a spring from each wall to a mass, and **one spring between the two masses**. All the masses are equal, and all the springs have the same stiffness. This system can vibrate in **two different ways**, which are called **modes**, and **a mode is just another word for a way of vibrating**.
children: In **Mode 1**, the masses move **together**. Both are pulled up and let go, and they rise and fall side by side, or in longitudinal motion they move left and right as a pair.
In **Mode 2**, the masses move **against each other**. One is pulled down and the other up, so whenever one rises the other falls.

A system can also vibrate in **both modes at the same time**. Pulling both masses up, but one higher than the other, makes them move together and against each other at once, which real movement and real speech production do all the time.

teaching.text: **When the masses go together, they move back and forth slowly, and when they go against each other, they move back and forth quickly**, so **Mode 2 has the higher frequency**. Both modes use the same masses and the same springs, so the explanation comes from asking **what each spring is actually doing**.
children: In **Mode 1**, the middle spring never stretches or compresses. It just rides along like a rigid bar, so **effectively Mode 1 has only two springs**.
In **Mode 2**, the middle spring is stretched and squished over and over, so **all three springs are working**, and Mode 2 has three units of stiffness instead of two.

**More stiffness means more pull back toward equilibrium, and more pull means a higher frequency.** In plain terms, a higher mode is not built from stiffer springs. It just makes the same springs do more stretching.

sections.title: Pop quiz

teaching.text: Adding a third mass adds a third way to vibrate, so **a system with three masses has three modes**. The modes are told apart the same way as before, by asking which masses move together and which move against each other.
children: All three masses can go back and forth together.
The two outer masses can move against each other while the middle mass stays still.
The middle mass can move against the two outer masses.
The more the masses go against each other, the more the springs stretch, so these three modes go from the lowest frequency to the highest.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: With **three masses** and four springs, the system has **three modes**, and each has its own frequency.
children: In **Mode 1**, all three masses go back and forth **together**, and this mode has the **lowest frequency**. The two middle springs just ride along, so they add no stiffness.

In **Mode 2**, the **middle mass stays still** while the two outer masses move against each other, and this mode has the **middle frequency**. To start it, the outer masses are pulled apart very carefully without touching the middle one.

In **Mode 3**, the **middle mass moves opposite to the two outer masses**, so **everything goes against everything else**. It has the most stretching and compressing, the most stiffness, and the **highest frequency**.

teaching.text: Because a mass acts only by moving, **changing one mass affects only the modes in which that mass moves**. Making the **middle mass heavier lowers the frequency of Mode 1 and Mode 3**, since the middle mass moves in both of them. **Mode 2 stays the same**, because in Mode 2 the middle mass does not move at all.
All three modes can also happen **at the same time**, and however the system is started, it vibrates as some mix of these **pure modes**.
children: **Learning a musical instrument means learning how to make the masses and springs vibrate in certain modes and not others.** How a string is plucked or a violin is bowed decides which modes get excited, and the favored modes are heard as **notes**.
A **trained singer** does the same with the vocal folds, controlling their mass and stiffness well enough to carry a tune.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: The pattern holds for any number of masses. **N masses give N independent modes**, so one mass has one way to vibrate, two masses have two, and six masses have six. Moving to higher modes, the pattern has **more reversals**, which are places where neighboring masses head in opposite directions, and more reversals mean more stretching, so **higher modes have higher frequencies**.
children: In chains of separate masses like these, the mode frequencies are generally **not whole-number multiples** of the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: The same mode looks alike no matter how many masses the chain has.
children: **Every Mode 1 is alike**, because all the masses go up and down together.
**Every Mode 2 is alike**, because the **left side goes against the right side**. With an odd number of masses, the middle one stays still.
**Every Mode 3 is alike**, because the **middle goes against the sides**.

teaching.text: Packing in more and more masses and springs, all the way to an **infinite number**, gives a **string**, like a guitar or piano string. **Every little piece of a string has mass, and every little piece stretches like a spring**, so a string has an infinite number of modes.
children: In the **lowest mode**, the whole string goes up and down together with hardly any stretching between its pieces, so it gives the **lowest note**.

A **building** is like a string that is fixed at the ground and free to sway at the top. Engineers design buildings to sway only in **Mode 1**, because in higher modes some floors would move one way while others moved the other way.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A **string fixed at both ends** with its lowest mode at **100 hertz** has its next modes at **200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz**, and **hertz** means times per second. These frequencies are **whole-number multiples** of the lowest one, and modes that line up this way are called **harmonics**.
The even spacing comes from how each mode is built out of the first one. **Mode 1 is a single bump**, and **Mode 2 is two copies of that bump**, with one half going up while the other half goes down.
children: With two copies, Mode 2 has **twice the stiffness** of Mode 1, so it has twice the frequency. Mode 3 fits three copies, and the fifth mode has **the first mode fitted into it five times**.
So with a lowest mode of 200 hertz, the fifth mode is five times 200.

teaching.text: A real string vibrates in **all of its modes at the same time**, and adding the separate motions together gives one complicated, changing shape. The **spectrum** of a sound tells **which frequencies are in it and how much of each there is**, with **frequency** along the horizontal axis and **amplitude** going up the vertical axis.
children: For the string moving in all five modes, the spectrum has **five evenly spaced spikes**. In this example the spikes have **equal height**, since nothing has filtered the sound.
If the string vibrated **only in Mode 3**, the spectrum would have **one spike at the frequency of Mode 3** and nothing else, which is like a **one-hot encoding**.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: **The vocal folds are even more complicated than strings.** They are a sheet of muscle, which is called a **membrane**, so their masses and springs spread across a surface instead of along a line. The same logic of modes still applies.
children: In **Mode 1**, the whole surface goes up and down together.
In **Mode 2**, the **left half goes against the right half**.
In **Mode 3**, the surface splits the other way, and the two halves on either side of a still middle line go against each other.
In **Mode 4**, four sections go against each other, and still higher modes get more and more complicated.

teaching.text: In real vocal folds, **all the modes happen at the same time**, so voicing produces a spectrum full of spikes. The evenly spaced frequencies attached to these membrane modes are teaching values, and the vocal folds are held fixed along their edges, so they **behave like a string**, which has evenly spaced harmonics.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: **The scientific method** depends on **very clear statements of how the world works**, usually written as **differential equations**. **Solving those equations gives a prediction** of what the world will be like when it is actually measured.
children: The **theory** is that the **vocal folds are a membrane**, so when they vibrate, the vibration has **equidistant peaks in its spectrum**, called **harmonics**.
The **prediction** is that **anyone's laryngeal vibration signal, when measured, will have a spectrum with equidistant harmonics.**

teaching.text: The prediction was tested by recording two voices in **Praat**, each made with the **mouth wide open** so that no particular vowel was being made.
children: In the first voice, the lowest spike was near **100 hertz**, and the next spikes fell close to two, three, four and five times that value, **evenly spaced just as predicted**.
In the second voice, the lowest spike was near **220 hertz**, and the next ones fell near twice and three times that value, again evenly spaced but farther apart.
**The prediction held for both voices**, so a theory built from simple masses and springs made a precise and correct prediction about real speech.

teaching.text: The second voice has a **higher pitch**, so those vocal folds are probably **smaller and thinner**. **Thinner folds have less mass, and less mass means a higher frequency**, so every harmonic is spaced farther apart.
children: This is part of how people are **recognized by their voices**, since each person's vocal folds give their voice its own spectrum.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A string can also be **fixed at one end and free at the other**, just like a **building**, which is fixed to the ground and free to sway at the top. The **fixed bottom** cannot move, so every mode has a point of **no motion** there, called a **node**, and the **free top** moves the most, called an **antinode**.
**Only the odd harmonics occur**, so the modes come at **100, 300, 500 and 700 hertz**, which are one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency.
children: **Mode 1** goes from no motion at the bottom to the most motion at the top, like a building swaying as a whole.
Two copies of Mode 1 would put a still point at both ends, which would make the system **fixed at both ends**, so that pattern is impossible here.
**Three copies** do end with free motion at the top, so the next mode has three times the frequency of Mode 1, and the mode after that holds five copies.
The simple version is that the free end must always be moving, and only an odd number of quarter-waves lands on a moving end.

teaching.text: When **both ends are fixed**, a string has **every whole-number multiple** of the lowest frequency, and when **one end is fixed and the other is free**, it has **only the odd multiples**.

lecture12.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization

teaching.text: The **2026 Nobel Prize in economics** went to **Robert Hall** and **Michael Woodford** for the **microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization**. **Stabilization** means getting a system to its equilibrium and keeping it there, which is the same job that **balancing feedback** does and the same thing a spring does when it pulls a mass back to rest.
children: In their model of the economy, **unemployment and inflation rise and fall in turns**, like the two curves of an oscillator, where one plays the role of position and the other plays the role of velocity.
The aim of stabilization policy is to **even out these peaks and troughs**, so the swings get smaller instead of producing high unemployment or runaway inflation.

teaching.text: Woodford's theory is called **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, or **DSGE**.
children: **Dynamic** means the economy changes over time according to rules.

**Stochastic** means the model can handle **random shocks**, such as a war starting or a large company's CEO being caught embezzling. This is close to stochastic gradient descent, where one odd data point can push the estimate far off, but later data pull it back toward the average.
**Equilibrium** means the goal is a steady state without wild jumps.

sections.title: One mass, two directions

teaching.text: A mass-spring system vibrates because **the spring wants to return to equilibrium** while **a moving mass wants to keep moving**. The same vibration can happen **longitudinally**, left and right along the spring, or **transversely**, up and down between two walls, and both kinds of motion behave in exactly the same way.
children: Understanding both is useful, because the vocal folds and the air in the vocal tract each vibrate most clearly in a different direction.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: **Raising the mass lowers the frequency**, so the system goes back and forth fewer times per second, and **raising the stiffness raises the frequency**, so it goes back and forth more times per second.
children: A heavier mass is harder to turn around, and a stiffer spring pulls back harder, which is why the two changes push the frequency in opposite directions.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: With **two masses** there are **two modes**. In **Mode 1** the masses move together, and in **Mode 2** they move against each other, and the system can also do both at once.
children: **Mode 1 is slower** because the middle spring just rides along without stretching, so effectively it has **only two springs**.
**Mode 2 is faster** because all **three springs** stretch and compress, and more working springs means **more stiffness** and a **higher frequency**.

teaching.text: Making the **middle spring stiffer** while the system vibrates leaves **Mode 1 unchanged**, since that spring never stretches in Mode 1. The same change makes **Mode 2 rise**, since in Mode 2 the middle spring stretches and compresses all the time.
children: In plain terms, a spring only matters in a mode where it is being stretched.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: With **three masses** there are **three modes**. In Mode 1 all three move together, in Mode 2 the middle mass is frozen while the outer two move against each other, and in Mode 3 the middle mass moves against both outer masses.

Making **Mass 2**, the middle mass, heavier **lowers the frequency of Mode 1 and Mode 3**, because the middle mass moves in both. The same change has **no effect on Mode 2**, because in Mode 2 the middle mass does not move at all.
children: **A mass affects frequency only through its movement.** If it does not move, it has no effect, if it moves a little, it has a small effect, and if it moves a lot, it has a large effect.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: **Every added mass adds one more mode**, and the same patterns repeat as the chain grows.
children: **Mode 1** is always everything going up and down together.
**Mode 2** always splits the system into **two parts** going against each other, and with an odd number of masses the middle mass is frozen.
**Mode 3** always splits the system into **three parts**, with the middle going one way and the sides the other.

teaching.text: Packing in more and more masses and springs gives a **string**. **Every little piece of a string has weight, which is its mass, and every little piece hates being stretched or compressed, which is its springiness.**
children: In musical instruments, these frequencies are heard as **notes**, and the ear can pick out many instruments at once because it is itself built of masses and springs.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A string fixed at both ends with its first mode at **100 hertz** has its next modes at **200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz**, so every mode is an **exact multiple** of the first. These multiples are called **harmonics**.
children: The second mode holds **two** copies of the first mode's bump, the third holds **three**, and the fifth holds **five**, so the frequency keeps multiplying by the number of copies that fit.

teaching.text: A single mode by itself is a **pure tone**, which sounds so annoying that it is used for sirens. What we normally hear has many modes at the same time, so a real string's motion looks erratic, much like the waveform of speech.
The **spectrum** shows the mixture, with **frequency** along the horizontal axis and **amplitude** up the vertical axis. For this string, it has spikes at 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: All of the results so far follow from a short set of **principles of mass-spring systems**, and each one follows from the others.
children: **Raising the mass lowers the frequency, and raising the stiffness raises the frequency.**
**A system with n masses has n modes of vibration**, and each higher mode has a higher frequency.
**An increase in mass lowers frequency in proportion to how much that mass moves**, which depends on where it is.
**Where there is maximal movement there is no stretching, and where there is maximal stretching there is no movement.**
**An increase in stiffness raises frequency in proportion to how much that spring stretches and compresses**, which also depends on where it is.

In a **fixed-fixed system**, the harmonics are **multiples of the base frequency**, because the base mode fits a whole number of times into each mode, and in a **fixed-free system** they are **odd multiples**, because it fits an odd number of times.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: Making one piece of a string **heavier**, such as thickening its very middle, changes some modes and not others.
children: In **Mode 1**, the middle moves up and down a lot, so the added mass **lowers** its frequency.
In **Mode 2**, the middle does not move at all, so the added mass changes **nothing**.
In **Mode 3** the middle moves again, so its frequency drops, and in **Mode 4** the middle is still again, so nothing changes. Going up the modes, the effect **alternates**.

teaching.text: **Motion and stretching alternate along a vibrating string.** Where a piece moves the most, it is just carried up and down and is hardly stretched, and where the string is stretched the most, such as right next to a fixed end, there is **no movement** at all.
children: **The shortcut is that maximal springiness is at the points of no movement.** In **Mode 5** of a string fixed at both ends, the string does not move at the **two fixed ends** or at the **four points where it crosses its middle line**, so those **six places** have the most springiness.
The **most motion**, and so the **least springiness**, is at the tops of the **five bumps**.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently

teaching.text: Changing one small piece of a string can push two modes in **opposite directions**. Take a spot where **Mode 4 is moving the most** and where **Mode 5 crosses its middle line**, so Mode 5 is not moving there at all, and raise both the **mass** and the **stiffness** of that piece.
children: **For Mode 4**, the piece is moving, so the extra mass **lowers** the frequency, and the piece is barely stretched, so the extra stiffness does nothing.
**For Mode 5**, the piece does not move, so the extra mass does nothing, and the piece is stretched the most, so the extra stiffness **raises** the frequency.
So the same change **lowers Mode 4's frequency and raises Mode 5's frequency**. Each mode is reasoned out on its own by asking whether the spot is moving or stretching in that mode.

teaching.text: This way of reasoning about small local changes, called **perturbation theory**, was first worked out with **drums** in the late nineteenth century by adding small amounts of **wax** to different spots.
children: Wax on a spot predicted to vibrate a lot added moving mass, and the drum's frequency was heard to **drop**.
Wax on a spot predicted not to move at all made **no difference** to the sound.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: The **larynx** holds the **vocal folds**, which form a **membrane** that is a bit like a drum, so they have many modes of vibration. In Mode 1 all the masses go up and down together, in Mode 2 the two halves go against each other, and the higher modes divide the surface into more and more parts.

Changes to the mass and stiffness of the vocal folds change the voice. People who smoke heavily can develop **nodules** on their vocal folds, which add mass at one spot and change the stiffness of nearby parts, so the folds vibrate differently and the voice sounds different.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: The **theory** is that the vocal folds vibrate in many modes at once, so a measured voice should have a spectrum with **equidistant harmonics**. A voice recorded and examined with **Praat** had its lowest harmonic at roughly 130 hertz, and the next harmonics fell close to twice and three times that value, so **the measurement matched the prediction.**
children: Each person's lowest frequency is different, but the harmonics above it are always close to multiples of it.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **building** is **fixed on one side and free on the other**, because it is fixed to the earth at the bottom while the top can sway in very high winds or an earthquake. Engineers design it to absorb that motion in **Mode 1**, which is unpleasant on a high floor but safe, and never in a higher mode, which would break the structure.

The **air inside the vocal tract** is also a fixed-free system. At the bottom, the **vocal folds are closed**, so the air **cannot move** and that end is **fixed**, and at the lips the air can go in and out easily, so that end is **free**.
children: Unlike a building, the air in the vocal tract vibrates in **all of its modes**, and speaking changes the masses and springs of different parts of the air.

teaching.text: A fixed-free system has **frequencies at 100, 300, 500 and 700 hertz**, jumping by odd steps. The first mode goes from **no motion** at the fixed end to **lots of motion** at the free end, which is only a quarter of a wave, and the next possible modes hold **three** and then **five** of these pieces.
children: Two pieces would end with no motion at both ends, which is a fixed-fixed pattern, so even multiples never occur.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract can be modeled as a **chain of masses and springs** that is fixed at the glottis end and free at the lip end. The masses stand for the air's inertia and the springs stand for its springiness.
children: The lowest mode is like the **first formant**, **F1**, and the next mode is like the **second formant**, **F2**. The frequencies of a fixed-free system are called **formants**, while those of a fixed-fixed system are called harmonics.
The second mode oscillates **three times faster** than the first, because it holds three of the first mode's quarter-wave pieces.

teaching.text: Three places along the tube matter for vowels. **/a/** is constricted **one third of the way from the glottis**, **/i/** is constricted **two thirds of the way from the glottis**, and **/u/** is constricted at the **free end at the lips**.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: A **constriction** is a place where the tongue or lips narrow the tract and squeeze the air, and the **glottis** is the tiny space between the vocal folds at the fixed end, so distances are measured from there.
children: In **done**, the central vowel, there is **no constriction**.
In **dean**, a **high front** vowel, the air is squeezed under the roof of the mouth, about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
In **Don**, a **low back** vowel, the air is squeezed far back in the throat, about **one third of the way from the glottis**.
In **dune**, a **high back** vowel made with **lip rounding**, the air is squeezed **at the lips**, and **Dan** is a **low front** vowel.

sections.title: Blank source page
Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: **Constricting air raises both its stiffness and its mass.** Squeezing air is like squeezing the air in a tire, which makes it **stiffer**, and packing air into a smaller volume raises its **density**, which makes it more **massive**.

It might seem that raising mass and stiffness together would **cancel out**. **That is false** for any system with many masses and springs, because each spot is either mostly **moving** or mostly **stretching** in a given mode.
children: At a spot with no motion and lots of stretching, only the extra stiffness counts, so the frequency **rises**.
At a spot with lots of motion and no stretching, only the extra mass counts, so the frequency **falls**.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: For **/u/**, rounding the lips squeezes the air at the **free end**, which raises the mass and the stiffness of the air there.
children: In **Mode 1**, the free end has lots of motion and almost no compression, so **motion dominates** and the extra mass lowers **F1**.
In **Mode 2**, the free end again has lots of motion, so **motion dominates** and the extra mass lowers **F2**.
So **both F1 and F2 go down**.

teaching.text: A speaker who started from the central vowel, with formants near 500, 1500 and 2500 hertz, and moved into /u/ showed **both formants dropping**, as predicted.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the air is squeezed about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**, and that one location acts differently in the two modes.
children: In **Mode 1**, this spot has lots of motion and hardly any compression, so **mass motion dominates** and the extra mass **lowers F1**.
In **Mode 2**, this spot has lots of compression, so **springiness dominates** and the extra stiffness **raises F2**.
In plain terms, the same squeeze lands on a moving spot for F1 and a springy spot for F2, so one formant falls while the other rises.

teaching.text: A speaker who went from the central vowel into /i/ showed the **first formant dropping a lot** and the **second formant going up**.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the air is squeezed about **one third of the way from the glottis**, and the pattern reverses.
children: In **Mode 1**, this spot near the fixed end has lots of compression, so **springiness dominates** and the extra stiffness **raises F1**.
In **Mode 2**, this spot has lots of motion, so **mass motion dominates** and the extra mass **lowers F2**.
So for /a/, **F1 goes up and F2 goes down**, and the two formants come closer together.

teaching.text: **If a constriction raises a formant a lot, the air at that spot must be springy and hardly moving in that mode**, and **if it lowers a formant a lot, the air there must be moving a lot**.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: The same principles explain the vowels. **Extra mass matters where the air moves, and extra stiffness matters where the air compresses and expands.** Because the vocal tract is fixed at the glottis and free at the lips, its formants are **odd multiples** of the lowest one.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: The air column can be modeled as **lines of air particles**, where each particle stands for billions of real air molecules, with the closed vocal folds at the **fixed end** and the open lips at the **free end**.
children: Where the lines bunch close together and spread far apart, the air is **compressing and expanding**, which is **springiness**.
Where the lines just move back and forth without changing their spacing, the air is acting as a **mass**, which is easiest to see at the **free end**.

teaching.text: **F1** has a single point of no motion, at the fixed end, **F2** has two, and **F3** has three. For the **schwa**, with no constriction, a measured voice had formants near **500, 1500 and 2500 hertz**, the odd multiples the theory predicts.
